A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same dataset and VLM-driven depth-fusion work, with readable text, equations, tables and figures. The supplied v1 ends with references; v4 includes Appendices A–C. Their added documentation can be compared without assuming that every newly described procedure is newly introduced.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on 3D-Visual-Illusion and Booster in Tables 1–2 and a Booster module ablation in Table 3.

after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds fine-tuning comparisons, Middlebury evaluation, confidence-map analysis, computational measurements and qualitative appendix studies.

M1.justification: The dual-branch prediction, flow-matching confidence and affine-alignment fusion remain. However, v4's introduction and Figure 4 depict RGB-only input to the VLM, replacing v1's RGB plus monocular and binocular maps, while v4 Section 4.2 still specifies all three inputs. This inconsistency prevents establishing whether the actual input procedure changed. Newly documented losses alone do not establish a method revision.

E1.justification: v4 extends evaluation beyond illusion-depth benchmarks to ordinary-scene generalization on Middlebury (Table 5) and qualitative 3D object detection using YOLO3D on real illusion images (Appendix C.5, Figure 15). These introduce a distinct scene regime and downstream task. The original five illusion categories remain.

E2.justification: The quantitative comparator sets in Tables 1–2 are unchanged; DA V2 abbreviates DepthAnything V2. Appendix Figure 12 adds a comparator labelled 'Moge' alongside the proposed method and existing depth baselines. YOLO3D is a downstream case study, not a competing depth-fusion method.

E3.justification: v4 adds fine-tuning versus no-fine-tuning controls, Sparse/Dense augmentation comparisons, half-resolution whole-image Middlebury evaluation without a maximum-disparity restriction, and an H100 resource benchmark at 1920×1080. Section 3 also replaces 178,912 training frames with 'over 200,000', although Appendix C.2 still lists components totaling 178,912; actual dataset expansion is unresolved.

E4.justification: The original module ablation is retained as Table 6. New analyses test whether fine-tuning monocular and stereo baselines resolves illusions, evaluate confidence-map errors under zero-shot transfer, and illustrate VLM recognition and downstream detection failures. These substantially expand the investigation of adaptation, reliability and failure modes.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. v4's approximately 20% confidence-map error evaluates a model output; it is not uncertainty reporting across experimental runs.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in the original Tables 1–2 and module ablation are unchanged. v4 adds substantial results: its Marigold fine-tuning comparison reports illusion-region EPE changing from 21.16 to 13.67 while bad2 worsens from 65.67 to 74.82; Middlebury EPE is 1.50 for the proposed method. Confidence error, additional stereo fine-tuning results, and 53,959 MB/4.77 s per iteration resource measurements are also newly reported.

T1.justification: The main geometric reasoning and Equations 1–10 are retained. Appendix A.2 explicitly formulates normalized constrained plane fitting, while Appendix B.1 defines weighted disparity losses and focal confidence supervision, including its binary target (Equations 11–14). These add mathematical specification, without new theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The dataset contribution, VLM-driven fusion contribution and headline SOTA claim remain. v4's introduction and conclusion add a more explicit mechanistic claim about complementary failure modes, including a generative-monocular versus discriminative-stereo characterization. This refines the scientific framing without replacing the central contributions.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations involving conflicting monocular priors and planar-label bias, acknowledges the ablation's EPE tradeoff, and introduces computational-cost and composite/novel-illusion limitations. The LoRA-potential caveat disappears. Booster interpretation changes from 'ours best' to favoring monocular methods, especially DepthPro, although unchanged Table 2 supports only region- and metric-specific advantages.

D1.justification: The appended material supplies loss definitions, data-processing pseudocode and thresholds, filtering/video-generation prompts, calibration details, LoRA targets, and training resources: four H100 GPUs, batch size six per GPU and approximately 20 days. Tables 1–2 explicitly identify fine-tuning status. v4 also adds direct dataset and model access links alongside the existing code link. These are major documentation additions, not evidence that all underlying procedures changed.

R1.justification: v4 adds references for Black Forest Labs' FLUX, Flask and Mousavian et al.'s 3D bounding-box estimation work. The stereo, monocular-depth and VLM related-work organization and most research positioning remain intact.

P1.justification: The introduction, dataset explanation, experimental narrative and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Separate dataset-result subsections are consolidated into 'Influence of 3D Visual Illusions', ablations are reorganized, and a dedicated discussion places expanded limitations before the conclusion. Appendices organize the additional technical material; author and publication information also change.

P2.justification: v4 redraws Figure 4, adds fine-tuning columns to Tables 1–2, introduces new experimental tables and appendix algorithm displays, and places the original Figures 5–6 side by side at reduced size. Appendix figures add pipeline, calibration, VLM and detection displays and extend qualitative comparisons, while reusing some original examples. The original ablation table is relocated and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially addresses v1's missing reproducibility documentation through included losses, processing algorithms, prompts and implementation details. New fine-tuning controls test whether ordinary adaptation suffices, while Middlebury and resource measurements clarify generalization and practical cost. These gains outweigh the remaining weaknesses, including inconsistent VLM-input descriptions and training-frame counts, and an overgeneralized Booster interpretation. The improvement rests on better methodological assessability and substantive controls, not higher scores in the unchanged original comparisons.
